en: Before we continue and get that HTML code
out of this file, it's time for a quick
summary on what we learned, because we
learned a lot. We learned about third-party
modules, which are essentially kind of the
same like standard library modules, just not
maintained by the core Deno team, but
instead by community members.
Just like the standard library though,
community Third-party modules can make
certain things easier. For example, the Oak
module here makes spinning up a web server
and reacting to requests much, much easier.
Now, speaking of that, here we are using the
Oak module.
We're creating an app with the application
constructor function, which is exposed by
that module.
And on that app object, we can register
middleware. Because the Oak library is a
middleware-driven framework.
Middleware-driven simply means that every
request is funneled through middleware until
all middleware functions have been
processed, at which time the response will
be sent back.
You can funnel requests from middleware to
middleware by calling the next method.
And if you have a middleware that does
something asynchronous, you should await
next to make sure that this middleware
doesn't send back the response too early.
A special kind of middleware, so to say, is
our router middleware created with the
router object.
This makes it very easy to register
different conditions for incoming requests
to execute some logic, some code only if
certain HTTP method and path combinations
are met. For example, here we return this
HTML code for GET requests to /nothing.
And we do this here, parse the request body
and redirect, if POST requests are sent to
/add-goal.
This, of course, is way more convenient than
what we had to do before where we manually
did all of that. And that's why we use
something like Oak in the end. Oak is a
great framework, a great third-party module,
and with it, handling requests simply is
much, much easier.
With that, however, we still have one
problem or one thing, one area that we can
improve, and that's the fact that our HTML
code is still hardcoded like this in our
TypeScript file.
This is not how we really wanna do that
because in realistic apps, we have way more
HTML code than just short snippets like this
one. Therefore, now we'll dive into
templates and templating engines.
